ABM Nurul Islam, Advocate -----For the Petitioner. 
Shahabuddin Ahmad, Deputy Attorney-General -----For the Respondents.
parties:
Kazi Mokhlesur Rahman ----- Petitioner
Vs
Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, Government of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Mozammel Hoque J: This Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why relieving of the petitioner from the responsibility of the office of the Government Pleader of Dhaka and appointment of respondent No. 4 as Government Pleader of Dhaka vide Annexure-A to the writ petition should not be declared to have been made and passed illegally and without any lawful authority (as per order dated 6-11-96). 

 2. It is the case of the petitioner that he was enrolled as an Advocate by the Bar Council on 22-12-1969. Thereafter he was enrolled as an Advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh in the year 1972 and became a Member of Bangladesh Supreme Court Bar Association in the year 1986. He was appointed as Additional Government Pleader for Dhaka District on 1-7-1991. Thereafter he was appointed as Government Pleader for Dhaka District on 12-11-1995. While the petitioner was discharging his functions as Government Pleader, Dhaka, he came to know that he has been relieved of his responsibility and in his place respondent No. 4 has been appointed as Government Pleader from Dhaka by an order issued under the signature of the respondent No. 3 which is Annexure-A to this Writ Petition. Further, it is stated that the petitioner is now aged about 55 years as his date of birth is 1st February, 1941 and he is entitled to serve as Government Pleader up to 60th year as per Clause 9, (11) of Chapter II of Legal Remembrance’s Manual, 1960 (hereinafter referred to LR Manual). It is further stated that respondent No. 4 who has been appointed as Government Pleader in his place is aged about 73 years and as such he is not entitled to be appointed as Government Pleader. It is further stated that this relieving of the present petitioner from the office of Government Pleader of the Dhaka District is absolutely illegal, without jurisdiction and violative of the principle of natural justice as well as the provisions of the LR Manual. 

 4. The petitioner had been functioning as Additional Government Pleader and while he was functioning as such, he was appointed as Government Pleader of Dhaka on temporary basis until further order by the order dated 12-11-95 which runs as follows: 

 5. After being appointed by the above by the above order he was discharging his function as Government Pleader of Dhaka. Thereafter, by the impugned order dated 17-7-96 he has been relieved of his responsibility as Government Pleader and in his place Advocate Mr. Foyezur Rahman Khan has been appointed as Government Pleader of Dhaka until further order. The aforesaid order dated 17-7-96 runs as follows: 

 It appears from both the orders quoted above that this letters of appointment and letter of removal were issued from the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. 

 6. Mr. ABM Nurul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that the provisions of the LR Manual have got the force of law and as such the same is enforceable in the Court of law and the Government is bound to follow the provisions of the LR Manual. He further submits that the aforesaid action of relieving the present petitioner from the officer of Government Pleader of Dhaka is absolutely arbitrary and malafide and as such the same has got no legal effect. His further submission is that in this case the principle of natural justice has been violated inasmuch as no notice was served upon the petitioner before passing the impugned order. It further submitted that violating the provisions of LR Manual the above order has been passed and, as such, the same has got no legal effect. 

 7. Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmad, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the Respondents, submits that the appointment of the present petitioner was a temporary one and knowing it fully well that it was a temporary appointment he accepted the office of the Government Pleader of Dhaka. He further submits that the provisions of the LR Manual have got no statutory force inasmuch as these are not framed or promulgated in pursuance of any Act or Ordinance or any other law. He submits that these are compilations of administrative orders, instructions and guide-lines made and given by the Government from time to time for appointment of Government Pleader and Public Prosecutor of the district in order to conduct the cases on behalf of the Government. Since no legal right has been violated, the question of violation of the principle of natural justice does not arise at all. He further submits that to change its lawyer is the discretion of the Government and since no legal right has been accrued and violated, the present writ application is not maintainable. 

 8. We have gone through the contents of the LR Manual, 1960 which show that Chapter I deals with Law Officers of the Government in the High Court and Chapter II deals with other law officers of the Government which means the Government Pleader, Public Prosecutor, Assistant Government Pleader and Assistant Public Prosecutor and specially appointed Government Pleader and Public Prosecutor whenever it is necessary for the Government. We are concerned with Chapter II, namely, the other law officers of the Government which means the Government Pleader and Public Prosecutor of the districts. Mr. ABM Nurul Islam submits that the provision of this LR Manual have got the force of law inasmuch as from time immemorial the provisions of LR manual have been followed in order to conduct the cases on behalf of the Government. Though it was compiled in the year 1960, yet before that even from the British Regime the posts of Government Pleaders and Public Prosecutors were there and they have been representing the Government in all civil, criminal and revenue cases of the Government. Since there is a long standing practice to follow the procedure of this LR Manual, this has got the force of law. Mr. Islam has referred to Article 152 of the Constitution which shows the definition of law as follows: 

 9. Since these provisions of LR Manual are being followed all along in the matter of conducting Government cases and also in appointment and removal of the Government Pleader and Public Prosecutor, this should be treated as law as contemplated under the Constitution. To this Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmad, the learned Deputy Attorney- General, submits that these provisions of LR Manual have not been formulated or passed in the form of Rules or Regulations in pursuance of and referring to any Act or Ordinance. He submits that there is no source of any legislation from which the provisions of LR manual have been originated. He submits that these are mere instructions, guide-lines and procedures laid down by the administrative orders of the Government from time to time in order to conduct the Government cases in civil, criminal and revenul matters and, as such, the same cannot be called 'Law' or the same have got the force of law. 

 10. Clause 9 of Chapter II of the LR Manual shows as to how appointment of Government Pleader is made from the lawyers concerned. Clause 8(8) of the aforesaid Manual shows that they are appointed by the Government for three years until it is renewed for any further period. Sub-clause (11) shows that the Government Pleader shall retire at the age of 60 unless on consideration of the report of the local authority Government considers that in the interest of the public service they should be retained for a further period. Clause 13 of the said Manual provides for filling up the temporary vacancy. Clause 14 of the said Manual provides leave of absence of the Government Pleader and Clause 16 shows about removal, suspension and other punishment. Clause 16 provides that whenever a Collector shall see cause to recommend the removal, suspension or other punishment of a Government Pleader, he shall submit a report on the facts of the case to the Legal Remembrancer through the Commissioner, and the Legal Remembrance shall, if he thinks fit, report the case for the orders of the Government in Judicial Department. In Miscellaneous Chapter, Clause 17 shows the appointment of the Public Prosecutor. The provisions of appointment and functions of the Government Pleader and Public Prosecutor are more or less same as provided in the LR Manual. 

 11.It is not disputed that these provisions of LR Manual are being followed by the Government for a long time past in the matter of conducting civil, criminal and revenue cases of the Government. But apparently, it lacks any source of law like any Act or Ordinance for its origination. So, in pursuance of any Act or Ordinance or any other Statute the provisions of LR Manual have not been made or codified. It clearly appears to us that these are Government instructions, guide-lines and procedures laid down by administrative orders made from time to time for appointment of Government Pleaders and Public Prosecutors as well as other procedure for conducting civil, criminal and revenue cases of the Government. In such a situation it is difficult to hold that the provisions of the LR Manual have got the force of law like other statutes. But it appears to us that though it is not law by itself, it has got some binding force in between the parties. As for example, if the fees of the Government Pleader are not paid, the Government. Pleader can claim the same in pursuance of these provisions which are laid down in the LR Manual. But, in fact, it cannot be said that these provisions are like other statutory laws or ordinance, as promulgated by the parliament. We have gone through the provisions of the LR Manual and it appears to us that no provision has been laid down anywhere as to how the Government Pleaders or the Public Prosecutors will be removed from the service like other officers of the Government. Only clause 16 shows that removal, suspension or other punishment may be made if the Collector sees causes to recommend for such removal, suspension or other punishment of a Government Pleader, then he shall submit it to the Commissioner who will again report it to the Legal Remembrancer and the Legal Remembrancer will take the matter before the Government for decision. This is the only provisions we find in the whole Manual of the Legal Rememberancer. 

 12. Learned Deputy Attorney-General submits that the Government Pleader is not holding an office of profit in the service of the Republic. He has referred to the case of Kazi Abdul Wahab vs. The Government of Bangladesh, 31 DLR 332. The learned Deputy Attorney-General submits that in that case the appointment and terms and conditions of service have been incorporated in President's Order 6 of 1972, that is, Law Officers' Order, 1972. The Deputy Attorney-General Kazi Abdul Wahab was removed from his service and he challenged the same in writ jurisdiction before this Court. Ultimately, it was held in that case that the Deputy Attorney- General is not holding any office of profit in the service of the Republic and, as such, he is not entitled to seek any relief in writ jurisdiction. Though the service conditions were guided under President's Order 6 of 1972, yet this Court held that the Law Officers are not holding any office of profit in the service of the Republic. Since the terms and conditions of service of the Government Pleaders and Public Prosecutors have not been laid down by any statutory provisions, the seeking of relief under writ jurisdiction regarding relieving of the present petitioner from the office of the Government Pleader is not called for and, as such, this writ petition does not lie before this Court inasmuch as no statutory provision has been violated in relieving of the present petitioner from the office of the Government Pleader. 

 13. Mr. Nurul Islam submits that the removal of the present petitioner is absolutely arbitrary and malafide and it also offends the principle of natural justice. Since no statutory provision of law has been violated in removing the present petitioner, the question of violation of the principle of natural justice does not arise at all. Further, the petitioner was appointed as Government Pleader on temporary basis until further order. The learned Deputy Attorney-General submits that since he was appointed on temporary basis as Government Pleader until further order and since the regular appointment has been made in the office of the Government Pleader, the question of arbitrary action or malafide action does not arise at all: We find substance in the above contention of the learned Deputy Attorney- General. The order of appointment dated 12-11-95 shows that the Additional Government Pleader Kazi Mokhlesur Rahman was appointed temporarily as Government Pleader until further order. The petitioner failed to produce any paper to show that he was appointed on a regular basis to the office of Government Pleader. The learned Deputy Attorney-General submits that since he was appointed on temporary basis until further order and since regular appointment has been made in favour of Mr. Foyezur Rahman Khan, Advocate, the question of any arbitrary action or malafide action does not arise at all. 

 14.He further submits that in this case the question of arbitrary or malafide action or violation of the principle of natural justice does not arise at all in view of the fact that the Government order dated 17-7-96 clearly shows that he was relieved of his duties from the office of temporarily appointed Government Pleader from Dhaka. No allegation of misconduct in service has been made in the impugned order. Since no allegation of any misconduct has been alleged in the impugned order, it cannot be said that the order of removeal is arbitrary or malafide or the principle of natural justice has been violated before passing the impugned orders. The petitioner knew it very well that while he was working as Additional Government Pleader, he was appointed temporarily until further order to the office of Government Pleader and knowing it very well that it was a temporary appointment he accepted the post. Now, he cannot claim that he was appointed on regular basis to the post of Government Pleader and, as such, he is legally entitled to maintain that post until he attains the age of 60 years. Further, while appointment was made, no time limit was given by the Government In this view of the matter we find that the letter of appointment of the petitioner has not created any vested legal right in his favour to the office of Government Pleader. Since the terms and conditions of service of the petitioner as Government Pleader have not been guided by any statutory legal provision, we hold that the petitioner cannot enforce any legal right in respect of holding the office of the Government Pleader in writ jurisdiction inasmuch as in removing him from the post of temporarily appointed Government Pleader, no statutory provision of law has been violated by the respondents. In this connection it may be mentioned that our above view finds support from the case of Talekhal Progressive Fishermen's Co-operative Society vs. Bangladesh, 1981 BLD (AD) 103. 

 15. Mr. Nurul Islam submits that in removing that petitioner from the post of Government Pleader the provisions of LR: Manual have been violated. But he failed to lay his finger on any provision of law to show that such and such provisions have been violated by the respondents in passing the impugned order. This is merely a vague and wild submission. 

 16. The learned Deputy Attorney-General submits that the Government Pleaders or the Public Prosecutors are the representatives of the Government to conduct and prosecute the cases on behalf of the Government in different Courts of the country. In fact, Government is the client and Government Pleaders and the Public Prosecutors are the lawyers. So, it is the discretion of the client to keep or change a lawyer according to its own desire. In the present case or in the case of Public Prosecutor though some Government instructions or guidelines or administrative orders are there for appointment of the Government Pleader and Public Prosecutor and also some provisions have been laid down for conducting the cases and for other relevant and ancillary matters in connection. with the Government cases the said provisions of the LR Manual have not give any statutory legal right to the post of Government Pleader or Public Prosecutor inasmuch as these provisions have got no force like any other Act, Ordinance or statute which we have discussed above. It is the discretion of the client to keep a lawyer or change a lawyer. In the instant matter even we do not find any malafide or arbitrary action of the Government. It was just a temporary appointment and in his place the Government appointed a regular Government Pleader and the very letter of appointment shows that it was a mere temporary appointment of the petitioner. It is well known to everybody that it is the pleasure of the client to keep or change his own lawyer for his interest This Court cannot direct the Government to retain any particular lawyer inasmuch as there is no such statutory or other legal proposition to give a direction like that. Since the provisions of the LR Manual have got no statutory force like other statutory laws, Rules or Regulations, we are of the view that the petitioner is not entitled to seek a direction from this Court that the Government should retain the present petitioner as Government Pleader inasmuch as there is no statute to make a direction like that. 

 17. Mr. Nurul Islam submits that the 2nd part of the impugned order provides that appointment of Advocate Mr. Foyezur Rahman Khan as the Government Pleader for Dhaka until further order. He challenges this appointment of Mr. Foyezur Rahman Khan alleging that he is above 60 years of age and, as such, he cannot be appointed as Government Pleader. The decision on this point is not called for in this writ jurisdiction inasmuch as this is not a writ petition in the form of quo-warranto. It is provided in the Manual that at the age of 60 the Government Pleader will retire. But there is a provision that if the Government desires or thinks, the period may be extended. So, it clearly appears from the Manual itself that it is upto the Government to appoint a Government Pleader or Public Prosecutor even after the age of 60 years. Since these provisions have got no statutory force and since this is not a writ petition in the form of quo-warrantoand since, prima-facie, it appears that the Government is at liberty to appoint its own lawyer even after the age of 60 years, we are of the view that this point does not call for any determination by this Court. 

 18. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case as well as the provisions of the LR Manual of 1960, we are of the view that the provisions of the Government Manual have got no force like other statutes and, as such, the present petitioner is not entitled to seek any relief under the writ jurisdiction from this Court. So, this Rule is liable to be discharged.
